column1: COMIG Pretender Prompt and Cue Audit — Results Summary
Descriptive pilot: 8 questions × 2 prompt conditions × 2 LLM judges × 2 presentation orders. No human participants.
Cases re-audited under final target rule
Primary cue family by prompt condition
Paired primary-cue change: 9/32 cells changed from style/form under naive to non-style under control, versus 1/32 in the reverse direction; exact two-sided McNemar p = 0.021.
Order-consistent selections were 9/10 Pretender under naive (Judge 1 n=2; Judge 2 n=8) and 9/9 under control (Judge 1 n=2; Judge 2 n=7). These aggregates are therefore dominated by Judge 2.

Style control changed the composition of stated primary cues: style/form primary cues fell from 10/32 to 2/32 (Wilson 95% intervals 0.18–0.49 and 0.02–0.20). In the paired comparison, 9 cells moved from style/form to non-style and 1 moved in the reverse direction (exact McNemar p=0.021). This change may partly reflect reduced availability of visible surface variation. We did not detect a prompt-condition difference in aggregate Pretender-as-human selections: 24/32 naive versus 25/32 controlled, with strongly overlapping Wilson intervals. Evaluator choice strongly affected selection stability (position flips: 12/16 versus 1/16), while the stable-pair aggregates were dominated by Judge 2.

Controlled responses omitted important content in all eight designated comparisons, and UNSPECIFIED-only justifications increased from 1/32 to 8/32. Event counts remain descriptive: style/form events fell from 2.31 to 0.91 per justification, while substantive/practical events were 2.91 versus 2.78. These counts capture stated cues under a 40–100-word justification limit, not every cue the judges may have used. I was the sole coder, and no independent second coder was used, so no inter-rater reliability statistic is available. The codebook and attribution rules were refined during coding, and J001–J064 were re-audited under the final target rule. Flipped pairs do not isolate position effects from stochastic run-to-run variability because each order was called once.

The controlled prompt matched anchor length and eliminated lists and headings, but first-person density moved farther from the anchors. Comma density was higher under style control in six of eight questions, which is consistent with possible artifact migration from bullets into sentence-internal enumeration. With only eight questions, this remains an exploratory observation rather than inferential evidence. Content was comparable in 5/8 designated pairs and confounded in 3/8, so the prespecified majority-confounded threshold was not met.
